snip.t: The pain is pleuritic, worsens on deep inspiration, and is accompanied by mild dyspnoea.

| Heart failure (pulmonary oedema) | Orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, elevated JVP, bibasal crackles, rapid onset dyspnoea | BNP elevated, chest X‑ray shows Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly; cough is usually dry, not productive mucus‑laden |

Alveolar‑capillary membrane – thin type I pneumocytes for gas exchange, type II cells produce surfactant: Infection fills alveoli with exudate → loss of surfactant → atelectasis and impaired O₂ diffusion, producing hypoxaemia and dyspnoea.
HIV: Pneumococcus, TB, PCP (dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, very low saturation, bilateral "ground-glass" infiltrates)
Symptoms: progressive dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain (may disappear as fluid separates the pleura), dry cough; plus symptoms of the cause (fever, weight loss, orthopnoea).
A 68‑year‑old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 30 %) presents with a 2‑week history of worsening dyspnoea on exertion and a dry, pleuritic left‑sided chest pain.
Air removal → sudden increase in pulmonary blood flow to previously collapsed alveoli → capillary leak → alveolar flooding → dyspnoea, pink frothy sputum.

| COPD | >40 y, long‑term smoking or biomass exposure; chronic productive cough, dyspnoea progressive, less diurnal variation | Fixed airflow obstruction (post‑bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC < 0.7) with < 12 % reversibility; emphysematous changes on CXR/CT |

qs.q: A 58‑year‑old postoperative patient has dyspnoea, dullness to percussion over the right lower zone, elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and tracheal shift toward the same side on X‑ray. What type of atelectasis is most likely?
qs.e: Pleural fluid or blood compresses the lung, producing elevation of the diaphragm and mediastinal shift toward the side of collapse. Resorption and contraction do not cause a shift toward the affected side.
qs.s: Introduction to Pulmonary Pathology and Atelectasis: MCQs

qs.q: A 54-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Examination reveals stony dullness at the left lung base with absent breath sounds. Which physical sign best helps differentiate this finding from right-sided heart failure?
o: Tracheal deviation away from the side of the fluid collection
Bilateral ankle oedema and elevated jugular venous pressure
Reduced tactile vocal fremitus over the lower zone
Stony dullness to percussion over the affected hemithorax
qs.e: Heart failure causes bilateral effusions accompanied by generalized systemic signs like elevated jugular venous pressure and oedema, whereas a unilateral effusion presents with localized examination findings. Stony dullness and reduced fremitus occur in both pleural effusions and consolidation.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with breast cancer presents with a recurrent right-sided pleural effusion causing severe dyspnoea. Fluid analysis shows a bloody appearance. Which measurement definitively confirms a haemothorax if suspected?
o: Pleural fluid cholesterol concentration exceeding serum levels
Pleural fluid pH falling below the critical threshold of 7.20
Pleural fluid haematocrit greater than 50% of peripheral blood
Pleural fluid triglyceride level greater than 110 mg/dL
qs.e: A bloody appearance is common in malignancy, but a true haemothorax is defined by a pleural fluid haematocrit that is greater than 50% of the patient's peripheral blood haematocrit. Triglycerides above 110 mg/dL identify chylothorax, not haemothorax.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with a massive right-sided pleural effusion is undergoing therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve severe dyspnoea. To prevent re-expansion pulmonary oedema, what safety precaution must the clinician observe?
o: Avoid draining more than 1.5 litres of fluid at any session
Ensure the patient lies strictly in the left lateral position
Check that the fluid pH remains consistently above 7.30
Administer intravenous loop diuretics before needle insertion
qs.e: Re-expansion pulmonary oedema can occur if too much fluid is removed too quickly, which is why clinicians avoid draining more than 1.5 litres at a single thoracentesis session. Diuretics do not prevent this mechanical complication of rapid lung expansion.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: An emergency department patient presents with severe dyspnoea and absent breath sounds on the left. Bedside thoracic ultrasound is performed as the gold standard imaging modality. What distinct advantage does ultrasound hold over standard chest radiography?
o: Detection of tiny fluid volumes as low as 20 mL and loculations
Measurement of pleural fluid pH and adenosine deaminase levels
Differentiation of transudate from exudate without thoracentesis
Definitive identification of pulmonary embolism and lung abscesses
qs.e: Bedside ultrasound can detect as little as 20 mL of fluid, identify septations and loculated pockets, and safely guide thoracentesis, outperforming upright chest X-rays. CT chest is required for detailed visualization of parenchymal causes like abscesses and pulmonary embolism.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 24-year-old tall, thin male presents with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Physical examination reveals hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the primary underlying pathological mechanism?
o: Alveolar rupture from positive ventilator pressure
Rupture of apical subpleural blebs or bullae
Perforation of a giant emphysematous bulla
Blunt trauma causing a major bronchial tear
qs.e: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in young, tall, thin males due to the rupture of apical subpleural blebs or bullae. Giant bullae are more characteristic of secondary causes or differential diagnoses like COPD, not primary spontaneous cases in healthy individuals.
qs.s: Pneumothorax: Classification, Clinical Features and Emergency: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman with a history of recurrent wheezing presents with severe dyspnoea. On examination, she has nasal polyps, and her symptoms are notably exacerbated whenever she takes pain medication for her headaches. Which underlying immunological mechanism best explains her presentation?
o: Direct beta-2 adrenergic receptor blockade on bronchial smooth muscle
Cyclooxygenase enzyme blockade shunting arachidonic acid towards leukotriene production
T-helper 2 lymphocyte activation mediated exclusively by Interleukin-4 production
Immunoglobulin E-mediated cross-linking on mast cells by environmental pollens
qs.e: Aspirin and NSAIDs block COX, shunting arachidonic acid to lipoxygenase and increasing leukotriene production which drives bronchoconstriction in Samter's triad. Beta-blockers cause bronchospasm through a different receptor mechanism.
qs.s: Bronchial Asthma: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis and GINA Stepwise: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a left-sided supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node), a persistent cough, and dyspnoea. Scrotal examination reveals a small, hard, painless intratesticular nodule. What do these systemic findings indicate?
qs.e: A supraclavicular node (left Virchow's node) and pulmonary symptoms like cough and dyspnoea are classic clinical manifestations of metastatic disease from a testicular tumour.
qs.s: Testicular Tumours, Hydrocele and Varicocele: MCQs

ai.title: Dyspnoea (Shortness of Breath)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dyspnoea is the subjective sensation of breathing difficulty. It requires a systematic bedside approach to identify life‑threatening causes, common tropical diseases, and appropriate investigations in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Dyspnoea is a patient‑reported feeling of uncomfortable breathing. Diagnosis starts with a focused history and physical exam, then targeted tests to confirm the underlying pathology.
b: Ask about onset, duration, triggers, and associated symptoms.
Assess severity with the Modified Borg Scale (0‑10).

sections.p: Severity guides urgency and level of care. Use the Borg scale and the WHO functional class for chronic disease.
b: Mild: Borg ≤ 3, no activity limitation.
Moderate: Borg 4‑6, limited daily activities.
Severe: Borg ≥ 7, requires urgent assessment.

sections.p: Categorise by organ system and consider local epidemiology.
b: Cardiac: acute decompensated heart failure, pericardial effusion.
Pulmonary: pneumonia, TB, PCP, asthma, COPD, pulmonary embolism.
Hematologic: severe anaemia, sickle‑cell crisis.
Metabolic: severe acidosis, electrolyte imbalance.
Psychogenic: anxiety, panic attack.

sections.p: Typical patterns help narrow the differential.
b: Orthopnoea & paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea → left‑sided heart failure.
Pleuritic pain, dry cough, fever → infection (TB, pneumonia, PCP).
Wheeze, prolonged expiration → obstructive airway disease.
Sudden onset, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia → pulmonary embolism.

t.b: Is oxygenation adequate? – SpO₂ < 92% suggests hypoxaemia; give supplemental O₂.
What structural abnormality is present? – Look for infiltrates, cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, pneumothorax.
Is there cardiac or pulmonary vascular involvement? – Signs of ischemia, right‑heart strain, or pericarditis.
Is anaemia or infection present? – Hb < 8 g/dL supports severe anaemia; leukocytosis suggests bacterial infection.
Is TB the cause? – Positive smear or GeneXpert confirms pulmonary TB.
What is the gas exchange status? – PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg indicates respiratory failure.

sections.p: Identify features that demand immediate intervention.
b: Sudden severe dyspnoea with chest pain → consider pneumothorax or massive PE.
SpO₂ < 85% despite O₂ → impending respiratory failure.
Altered mental status, hypotension, or new arrhythmia → cardiac collapse.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.
b: Oxygen: titrate to SpO₂ ≥ 94% (≤ 88% in COPD).
Diuretics (e.g., furosemide) for fluid overload in heart failure.
Bronchodilators (short‑acting β2‑agonist) for asthma/COPD exacerbations.
Antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia; anti‑TB regimen for confirmed TB.
Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for PCP in HIV patients.
Analgesia (paracetamol) for pleuritic pain; avoid NSAIDs in severe renal disease.

sections.p: Arrange review based on cause and severity.
b: Heart failure: review in 1 week, optimise diuretics, counsel on salt restriction.
TB: ensure directly observed therapy, monitor sputum conversion.
COPD: smoking cessation, inhaler technique check, vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic dyspnoea but have distinct management.
b: Chest pain from myocardial infarction – focus on ECG and cardiac enzymes.
Anxiety‑related hyperventilation – look for normal oxygenation and psychosocial triggers.
Anemia‑related fatigue – check hemoglobin; treat with transfusion if severe.
Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude early pulmonary embolism.
Mild leukocytosis may be absent in HIV‑related infections.
SpO₂ can be falsely high in carbon monoxide poisoning.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset severe dyspnoea with chest pain or syncope
Rapidly rising respiratory rate > 30/min with use of accessory muscles

faq.q: Why does heart failure cause dyspnoea?
faq.a: Elevated left‑ventricular pressure backs up into pulmonary veins, causing interstitial oedema that stiffens the lung and impairs gas exchange.

faq.q: When is a chest X‑ray essential?
faq.a: In any acute dyspnoea to look for pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, or cardiomegaly, especially when bedside ultrasound is unavailable.

faq.q: Can TB present with isolated dyspnoea?
faq.a: Yes; primary or re‑activation TB may cause progressive dyspnoea with a dry cough and normal early X‑ray, so sputum testing is crucial in endemic areas.

exam: What immediate bedside maneuver distinguishes a tension pneumothorax from severe asthma? — Look for absent breath sounds, hyper‑resonance, and tracheal deviation; treat with needle decompression.

A 45‑year‑old farmer with chronic cough presents with worsening dyspnoea; what is the most likely diagnosis and why? — COPD from biomass exposure; chronic productive cough, FEV₁/FVC <0.7, limited reversibility.

How would you prioritize investigations for a HIV‑positive patient with dyspnoea and dry cough in a district hospital? — Pulse oximetry, bedside ultrasound, sputum GeneXpert, and if possible ABG; treat PCP if SpO₂ < 92% and chest X‑ray shows ground‑glass.

Why is a high‑dose diuretic preferred over a vasodilator in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema? — Diuretics remove excess fluid rapidly, reducing pulmonary capillary pressure; vasodilators may worsen hypotension.

Explain the pathophysiological reason for orthopnoea in left‑sided heart failure. — Supine position increases venous return, raising pulmonary capillary pressure and causing fluid transudation, worsening breathlessness.
What are the red‑flag signs that convert a stable dyspnoea presentation into an emergency? — Sudden severe dyspnoea, SpO₂ <85%, hypotension, altered mental status, and signs of shock.

When is non‑invasive ventilation indicated for dyspnoea, and why might it be unavailable in low‑resource settings? — Indicated for hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD exacerbation) when PaCO₂ >45 mmHg and pH <7.35; lack of machines or electricity limits use.

How does anemia cause dyspnoea, and when should you transfuse in a low‑resource hospital? — Reduced oxygen‑carrying capacity forces higher cardiac output and ventilation; transfuse when Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic with tissue hypoxia.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam allow rapid discrimination between cardiac, pulmonary, haematologic and psychogenic dyspnoea, even where investigations are limited.
b: Onset: sudden (PE, pneumothorax) vs gradual (CHF, COPD, anaemia).
Duration: minutes‑hours (acute) vs days‑weeks (chronic).
Triggers: exertion, lying flat, allergens, recent surgery, travel, infection symptoms.
Associated symptoms: chest pain, cough, fever, wheeze, orthopnoea, PND, haemoptysis, leg swelling, anxiety.
Context: HIV status, TB exposure, pregnancy, recent blood loss, medication use (NSAIDs, opioids).
Severity: Modified Borg Scale (0‑10) and WHO functional class for chronic disease.
Red‑flag queries: syncope, altered mental status, hypotension, SpO₂ < 85 % on room air.

t.b: Look for use of accessory muscles, tripod position, cyanosis, clubbing, chest wall deformities; positive indicates increased work of breathing or chronic hypoxia.
Feel for vibration over bronchi; increased fremitus suggests consolidation, decreased suggests pleural effusion or pneumothorax; cannot differentiate cause of consolidation.
Dullness = fluid or consolidation; hyper‑resonance = air‑filled space (pneumothorax, emphysema); cannot quantify volume of fluid.
Crackles (fluid, fibrosis), wheeze (airway obstruction), pleural rub (pleuritis), absent breath sounds (large effusion or pneumothorax); cannot assess severity of obstruction.
Measure bilateral movement; asymmetry suggests unilateral pathology (effusion, pneumothorax, lobar collapse).
Elevated JVP indicates right‑sided pressure overload (CHF, PE); normal JVP does not exclude left‑sided failure.
Suggest systemic congestion; absent does not rule out early cardiac dyspnoea.
Detect B‑lines (interstitial edema), pleural sliding (rules out pneumothorax), effusion size; cannot replace formal chest X‑ray for detailed anatomy.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that answer a specific clinical question; use algorithms that adapt when a test is unavailable.
b: Pulse oximetry – immediate oxygenation status; SpO₂ < 94 % (≥ 88 % in COPD) triggers supplemental O₂.
Chest X‑ray – first‑line imaging; look for infiltrates, effusion, pneumothorax, cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion.
ECG – screens for ischemia, arrhythmia, right‑heart strain; new ST changes suggest cardiac cause.
Full blood count – anaemia (Hb < 8 g/dL) or leukocytosis; severe anaemia explains dyspnoea, triggers transfusion.
Serum electrolytes & renal function – detect metabolic acidosis, hyper‑kalaemia, renal failure that may worsen dyspnoea.
Arterial blood gas (if available) – assess PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH; PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg guides ventilation support.
D‑dimer – rule‑out PE in low‑risk patients; negative (< 500 ng/mL) essentially excludes PE.
Sputum microscopy (Ziehl‑Neelsen) – for TB in HIV‑positive or chronic cough; positive confirms mycobacterial infection.
HIV rapid test – influences differential (TB, PCP, lymphoma).
Echocardiography (portable) – evaluates LV function, pericardial effusion; EF < 40 % supports heart failure.

t.a: Chest X‑ray – What is the anatomic cause?
t.b: Consolidation = pneumonia/TB; fluid level = pleural effusion; absent lung markings + hyper‑lucency = pneumothorax; cardiomegaly = chronic heart failure.
Result < 500 ng/mL in low‑risk patient rules out PE; if ≥ 500 ng/mL proceed to CT‑PA or bedside ultrasound.

t.a: Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) – Not directly for dyspnoea but for pleural fluid analysis.
t.b: SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates transudate (CHF, cirrhosis); < 1.1 g/dL indicates exudate (infection, malignancy).

t.a: Pleural fluid analysis – What type of effusion?
t.b: Light’s criteria: pleural protein/serum protein > 0.5 or LDH ratio > 0.6 or pleural LDH > 2/3 upper normal = exudate; exudate + lymphocyte predominance suggests TB.
PaO₂ < 60 mmHg = hypoxemia; PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg = hypercapnia; pH < 7.35 with high PaCO₂ indicates need for ventilation support.
EF < 40 % or right‑ventricular dilation with McConnell’s sign supports heart failure or massive PE; absent findings shift focus to pulmonary causes.

t.a: Point‑of‑care ultrasound – Does lung sliding exist?
t.b: Absent sliding with lung point = pneumothorax; multiple B‑lines = interstitial edema; cannot replace CT for detailed PE assessment.
Rely on bedside clinical algorithm: e.g., if ABG unavailable, use SpO₂ < 85 % and mental status to decide on ventilation; if D‑dimer unavailable, use Wells score to decide on imaging.

sections.p: Combine history, exam and targeted investigations to place dyspnoea into a recognised classification that guides urgency and treatment.
b: Acute severe dyspnoea with SpO₂ < 85 % or altered mental status = emergency; immediate airway, O₂, and cause‑specific therapy.
Moderate dyspnoea (Borg 4‑6) with stable vitals = urgent assessment; admit if underlying cardiac or pulmonary disease likely.
Mild dyspnoea (Borg ≤ 3) with no organ dysfunction = outpatient work‑up unless red‑flags present.
WHO functional class I‑IV for chronic disease: I = no limitation, IV = symptoms at rest; used for COPD, asthma, heart failure.
PE severity index (PESI) – low‑risk (class I‑II) may be managed outpatient if resources allow; high‑risk (≥ III) requires admission.
Heart failure NYHA class I‑IV aligns with Borg scale; NYHA III‑IV often need diuretics and possible NIV.
TB severity: smear‑positive pulmonary disease with extensive infiltrates = high transmission risk; start isolation and treatment promptly.

sections.p: Several entities mimic dyspnoea; a focused comparison table helps avoid misdiagnosis.

t.b: Unilateral hyper‑resonance, absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation (late) point to tension; asthma shows diffuse wheeze, prolonged expiration, normal percussion.
Effusion: dullness, decreased tactile fremitus, fluid level on X‑ray; atelectasis: bronchial breath sounds, increased fremitus, shift toward side of collapse.
PE: pleuritic pain, tachycardia, clear lungs, normal or low fever; pneumonia: productive cough, fever, localized crackles, infiltrate on X‑ray.
Anemia: low Hb, normal cardiac exam, high-output signs; heart failure: elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray.
Anxiety: rapid shallow breathing, normal ABG or mild respiratory alkalosis; metabolic acidosis: low pH, low HCO₃⁻, compensatory hyperventilation.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides acute and chronic dyspnoea care, beginning with airway, oxygen and immediate safety, then addressing the underlying cause, monitoring response and escalating when thresholds are crossed.
b: 1. Assess airway and breathing; give high‑flow O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 % (≤ 88 % in COPD).
2. Position upright, give bronchodilator inhaler (short‑acting β2‑agonist ± anticholinergic) if wheeze present.
3. If cardiac cause suspected, start loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) and consider IV nitrates; avoid pure vasodilators in preload‑dependent shock.
4. For suspected infection, start empiric antibiotics covering local pathogens (e.g., TB, bacterial pneumonia, PCP) after cultures if possible.
5. Initiate anticoagulation (low‑molecular‑weight heparin) when pulmonary embolism is likely and no contraindication.
6. Monitor vitals, urine output, repeat SpO₂, and mental status every 15 min initially; watch for rising lactate or worsening acidosis.
7. Escalate to non‑invasive ventilation if SpO₂ < 85 % despite O₂, respiratory rate > 30, or PaCO₂ rising; intubate if mental status deteriorates.
8. Refer to higher‑level centre for tension pneumothorax, massive hemothorax, or refractory shock.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects, drug‑drug interactions and mitigation strategies for the medicines most often used in dyspnoea.
b: Loop diuretics may cause hypokalaemia; give potassium‑sparing agent or replace K⁺ if serum < 3.5 mmol/L.
β2‑agonists can provoke tachycardia and hypokalaemia; monitor heart rate and electrolytes, avoid in severe arrhythmia.
Anticholinergics may precipitate urinary retention in elderly; assess bladder function before use.
Heparin can cause heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia; check platelet count after 5‑7 days, switch to alternative if falling >50 %.
Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin) prolong QT; avoid with other QT‑prolonging drugs and monitor ECG if baseline QT > 450 ms.
Corticosteroids raise blood glucose; monitor glucose in diabetics and adjust insulin accordingly.
Nitroglycerin may cause severe hypotension in hypovolaemic patients; ensure adequate preload before administration.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of deterioration that demand rapid escalation or transfer.
b: SpO₂ persistently < 85 % despite maximal O₂ → start NIV or intubation.
Respiratory rate ≥ 30 /min with use of accessory muscles → consider NIV.
New or worsening altered mental status → airway protection, urgent transfer.
Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg → treat shock, consider inotropes, refer.
Rapid rise in serum lactate (> 2 mmol/L) or worsening acidosis → investigate sepsis or tissue hypoxia, escalate care.
Development of new chest pain with unilateral absent breath sounds → suspect tension pneumothorax, perform immediate needle decompression.

sections.p: Conditions that modify presentation, investigations or treatment of dyspnoea in low‑resource settings.
b: HIV infection: higher risk of PCP, TB and opportunistic infections; CD4 count guides prophylaxis, sputum GeneXpert if available.
Malnutrition lowers albumin, may mask pleural effusion size on ultrasound; use bedside thoracic tap for diagnosis.
Pregnancy: physiological dyspnoea, avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., ACE inhibitors); use low‑dose steroids cautiously.
Diabetes: steroids and β2‑agonists raise glucose; monitor capillary glucose frequently.
Herbal remedies (e.g., kava) can depress respiration; ask about use and discontinue if respiratory depression present.
Alcohol excess predisposes to aspiration pneumonia and cardiomyopathy; consider liver function when prescribing diuretics.
Renal failure limits loop diuretic clearance and may cause fluid overload; use cautious dosing and monitor electrolytes.
Liver failure reduces synthesis of clotting factors; avoid invasive thoracentesis without correction of coagulopathy.

sections.p: Tailored approaches for vulnerable populations and settings with limited resources.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate respiratory scores (e.g., WHO pneumonia score); avoid adult‑dose diuretics, give nebulised salbutamol with spacer.
Pregnant women: prioritize maternal oxygenation, use low‑molecular‑weight heparin for PE, avoid ACE inhibitors and high‑dose diuretics.
Elderly: start diuretics low‑dose, watch for orthostatic hypotension; prefer inhaled bronchodilators over systemic β‑agonists.
People with HIV: start cotrimoxazole prophylaxis if CD4 < 200, treat PCP with high‑dose TMP‑SMX, consider adjunctive steroids for severe disease.
Low‑resource hospitals: use bedside ultrasound for pleural effusion, pneumothorax and IVC assessment; rely on clinical scoring when labs unavailable.

facts: Modified Borg Scale 0‑10: ≤3 mild, 4‑6 moderate, ≥7 severe
Pneumothorax: unilateral hyper‑resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation late
PE: sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia, normal chest auscultation
Atelectasis: dullness, decreased breath sounds, shift toward affected side
Hemothorax: bloody fluid, low haemoglobin, hypotension
COPD exacerbation: prolonged expiration, wheeze, use of accessory muscles
Anemia: dyspnoea when Hb <8 g/dL in low‑resource settings

vivas.q: What bedside manoeuvre distinguishes tension pneumothorax from severe asthma?
vivas.a: Check for unilateral hyper‑resonance and absent breath sounds; absence of wheeze and presence of tracheal deviation favour pneumothorax.

vivas.q: A 45‑year‑old farmer with chronic cough presents with worsening dyspnoea; what is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Pulmonary tuberculosis, given chronic cough, low‑resource setting and high prevalence.

vivas.q: How would you prioritise investigations for an HIV‑positive patient with dyspnoea and dry cough?
vivas.a: Start with chest X‑ray, sputum microscopy for AFB, pulse oximetry, and CBC; if hypoxia or abnormal X‑ray, add ABG and consider empiric TB treatment.

vivas.q: Why is a high‑dose diuretic preferred over a vasodilator in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema?
vivas.a: Diuretics reduce preload and pulmonary congestion rapidly; vasodilators may worsen hypotension and are less effective in low‑output states.

vivas.q: Explain the pathophysiological reason for orthopnoea in left‑sided heart failure.
vivas.a: Left ventricular failure increases pulmonary venous pressure; lying flat raises venous return, worsening pulmonary congestion and causing dyspnoea.

vivas.q: What red‑flag signs convert a stable dyspnoea presentation into an emergency?
vivas.a: SpO₂ <85% despite O₂, altered mental status, hypotension, new arrhythmia, sudden severe chest pain, or signs of tension pneumothorax.

vivas.q: When is non‑invasive ventilation indicated for dyspnoea, and why might it be unavailable in low‑resource settings?
vivas.a: Indicated in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD) or early cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; may be unavailable due to cost, lack of equipment, or training.

vivas.q: How does anemia cause dyspnoea, and when should you transfuse in a low‑resource hospital?
vivas.a: Reduced oxygen carrying capacity leads to tissue hypoxia; transfuse if Hb <8 g/dL or symptomatic despite correction of causes.

vivas.q: A 58‑year‑old postoperative patient has dyspnoea, dullness to percussion over the right lower zone, elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and tracheal shift toward the same side on X‑ray. What type of atelectasis is most likely?
vivas.a: Lobar atelectasis of the right lower lobe; the shift toward the affected side reflects collapse.

vivas.q: A 54‑year‑old man presents with a 2‑week history of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Examination reveals stony dullness at the left lung base with absent breath sounds. Which physical sign best helps differentiate this?
vivas.a: Absent breath sounds with dullness suggests pleural effusion; a positive fluid thrill or shifting dullness would confirm a large effusion.

vivas.q: A 50‑year‑old woman with breast cancer presents with a recurrent right‑sided pleural effusion causing severe dyspnoea. Fluid analysis shows a bloody appearance. Which measurement definitively confirms a haemothorax if suspected?
vivas.a: Pleural fluid haemoglobin >50 g/L or pleural fluid/serum haemoglobin ratio >0.5 confirms haemothorax.

vivas.q: A 70‑year‑old man with a massive right‑sided pleural effusion is undergoing therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve severe dyspnoea. To prevent re‑expansion pulmonary oedema, what safety precaution must the clinician observe?
vivas.a: Remove no more than 1.5 L at a time and monitor for sudden dyspnoea; avoid rapid large‑volume drainage.

vivas.q: An emergency department patient presents with severe dyspnoea and absent breath sounds on the left. Bedside thoracic ultrasound is performed as the gold standard imaging modality. What distinct advantage does ultrasound have?
vivas.a: Rapid bedside diagnosis, no radiation, can detect pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and lung sliding in real time.

vivas.q: A 24‑year‑old tall, thin male presents with sudden‑onset right‑sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Physical examination reveals hyper‑resonance and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the primary underlying pathology?
vivas.a: Spontaneous primary pneumothorax due to rupture of subpleural blebs.

vivas.q: A 28‑year‑old woman with a history of recurrent wheezing presents with severe dyspnoea. On examination she has nasal polyps, and her symptoms are notably exacerbated whenever she takes pain medication for her headaches.
vivas.a: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or aspirin‑exacerbated respiratory disease; NSAIDs trigger bronchospasm.

vivas.q: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a left‑sided supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Virchow's node), a persistent cough, and dyspnoea. Scrotal examination reveals a small, hard, painless intratesticular nodule. What do these findings suggest?
vivas.a: Metastatic carcinoma (likely testicular) with widespread lymphatic spread; consider staging and palliative care.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in a patient with acute dyspnoea and SpO₂ 80% on room air?
A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism has a Wells score of 4.5. What is the next best step?
Which sign is NOT typical of tension pneumothorax?
o: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side

mcqs.q: In a patient with COPD exacerbation, which drug is contraindicated in the presence of severe hypoxaemia?
Which investigation is most useful to differentiate pleural effusion from atelectasis?

cases.v: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with sudden dyspnoea, chest pain, and tachycardia. She is a smoker, has no known cardiac disease, and reports a recent hiking trip. Examination shows unilateral hyper‑resonance and absent breath sounds on the left. SpO₂ 88% on 2 L O₂.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: Lung ultrasound showing absent lung sliding
Insert a small‑bore needle or chest tube to evacuate air

cases.v: A 65‑year‑old man with known COPD presents with worsening dyspnoea, productive cough, and fever. He is on long‑acting bronchodilators. Examination shows bilateral wheeze, use of accessory muscles, and SpO₂ 90% on 2 L O₂. Chest X‑ray shows hyperinflated lungs with a new infiltrate.

qs.q: What is the most likely complication?
qs.a: Acute exacerbation of COPD with possible pneumonia

qs.q: Which investigation will guide antibiotic choice?
What is the first step in management?
qs.a: Administer nebulised bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids

mistakes: Assuming all dyspnoea is cardiac; ignoring pulmonary causes
Using high‑dose vasodilators in acute pulmonary oedema
Treating anaemia with transfusion only when Hb <4 g/dL
Overlooking the need for oxygen titration in COPD
Failing to recognise tracheal deviation as a late sign of tension pneumothorax
Misinterpreting pleural fluid haemoglobin as a diagnostic criterion without ratio
Not using ultrasound to differentiate effusion from atelectasis
Assuming all pleural effusions are malignant in cancer patients
exam: What bedside manoeuvre distinguishes tension pneumothorax from severe asthma? — Check for unilateral hyper‑resonance and absent breath sounds; absence of wheeze and presence of tracheal deviation favour pneumothorax.
A 45‑year‑old farmer with chronic cough presents with worsening dyspnoea; what is the most likely diagnosis? — Pulmonary tuberculosis, given chronic cough, low‑resource setting and high prevalence.

How would you prioritise investigations for an HIV‑positive patient with dyspnoea and dry cough? — Start with chest X‑ray, sputum microscopy for AFB, pulse oximetry, and CBC; if hypoxia or abnormal X‑ray, add ABG and consider empiric TB treatment.

Why is a high‑dose diuretic preferred over a vasodilator in acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema? — Diuretics reduce preload and pulmonary congestion rapidly; vasodilators may worsen hypotension and are less effective in low‑output states.

Explain the pathophysiological reason for orthopnoea in left‑sided heart failure. — Left ventricular failure increases pulmonary venous pressure; lying flat raises venous return, worsening pulmonary congestion and causing dyspnoea.

What red‑flag signs convert a stable dyspnoea presentation into an emergency? — SpO₂ <85% despite O₂, altered mental status, hypotension, new arrhythmia, sudden severe chest pain, or signs of tension pneumothorax.

When is non‑invasive ventilation indicated for dyspnoea, and why might it be unavailable in low‑resource settings? — Indicated in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD) or early cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; may be unavailable due to cost, lack of equipment, or training.

How does anemia cause dyspnoea, and when should you transfuse in a low‑resource hospital? — Reduced oxygen carrying capacity leads to tissue hypoxia; transfuse if Hb <8 g/dL or symptomatic despite correction of causes.

A 58‑year‑old postoperative patient has dyspnoea, dullness to percussion over the right lower zone, elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and tracheal shift toward the same side on X‑ray. What type of atelectasis is most likely? — Lobar atelectasis of the right lower lobe; the shift toward the affected side reflects collapse.

A 54‑year‑old man presents with a 2‑week history of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Examination reveals stony dullness at the left lung base with absent breath sounds. Which physical sign best helps differentiate this? — Absent breath sounds with dullness suggests pleural effusion; a positive fluid thrill or shifting dullness would confirm a large effusion.

A 50‑year‑old woman with breast cancer presents with a recurrent right‑sided pleural effusion causing severe dyspnoea. Fluid analysis shows a bloody appearance. Which measurement definitively confirms a haemothorax if suspected? — Pleural fluid haemoglobin >50 g/L or pleural fluid/serum haemoglobin ratio >0.5 confirms haemothorax.

A 70‑year‑old man with a massive right‑sided pleural effusion is undergoing therapeutic thoracentesis to relieve severe dyspnoea. To prevent re‑expansion pulmonary oedema, what safety precaution must the clinician observe? — Remove no more than 1.5 L at a time and monitor for sudden dyspnoea; avoid rapid large‑volume drainage.

An emergency department patient presents with severe dyspnoea and absent breath sounds on the left. Bedside thoracic ultrasound is performed as the gold standard imaging modality. What distinct advantage does ultrasound have? — Rapid bedside diagnosis, no radiation, can detect pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and lung sliding in real time.

A 24‑year‑old tall, thin male presents with sudden‑onset right‑sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. Physical examination reveals hyper‑resonance and absent breath sounds on the right. What is the primary underlying pathology? — Spontaneous primary pneumothorax due to rupture of subpleural blebs.
